contract_plain_english: For any N, any real bound K (implicitly positive), and any independent, mean-zero random variables X_1, ..., X_N satisfying the uniform bound |X_i| <= K for every i, set sigma^2 = E X_1^2 + ... + E X_N^2 (the sum of second moments, which equals the variance of the sum because the terms are independent and mean zero). Then for every real t >= 0, the probability that the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the plain sum X_1 + ... + X_N is at least t is at most 2 exp( - (t^2 / 2) / (sigma^2 + K t / 3) ). Unlike Theorems 2.8.1-2.8.3, this bound contains no absolute constant at all: the prefactor 2, the 1/2 in the numerator, and the 3 in the term K t / 3 are explicit numbers, and there is no minimum of two branches — a single fraction interpolates between a gaussian tail governed by the true variance and an exponential tail governed by K. Boundedness replaces sub-exponentiality here and is explicitly the stronger hypothesis; no proof is given in the text, it being delegated to Exercises 2.8.5 and 2.8.6.

Then, for every t >= 0, we have P{ |sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i| >= t } <= 2 exp( - (t^2/2) / (sigma^2 + K t / 3) ). Here sigma^2 = sum_{i=1}^{N} E X_i^2 is the variance of the sum.' The absolute-value bars around the sum are visible in the rendered page; the source wording 'such that |X_i| <= K all i' omits 'for'.

'Let us mention a strengthening of Bernstein's inequality that is sensitive to the variance of the sum. It holds under the stronger assumption that the random variables X_i are bounded.' — the boundedness hypothesis replaces sub-exponentiality and is explicitly described as stronger.
'We leave the proof of this theorem to the next two exercises.' — no proof is given in the text; Exercises 2.8.5 and 2.8.6 supply it.
